html:
Russia's second city, at the mouth of the Neva on the Baltic Sea, built from 1703 by Peter the Great and the capital of the Russian Empire for two centuries.

Peter took the marshy delta from Sweden during the Great Northern War and founded the city in 1703 as a port and a "window on Europe". Forced labourers by the tens of thousands drained the land, and many died. He moved the capital from Moscow in 1712. Italian and French architects gave it straight avenues, canals and stone palaces. Catherine the Great began the art collection of the Hermitage in the Winter Palace.

In the 1800s it was the stage of Russian literature and science. Fyodor Dostoevsky set Crime and Punishment in its poor quarters, and Dmitri Mendeleev drew up the periodic table at its university in 1869.

Renamed Petrograd in 1914, it was the cradle of the Russian Revolution of 1917. The Bolsheviks moved the capital back to Moscow in 1918, and in 1924 the city became Leningrad. In the Second World War German and Finnish forces besieged it for nearly 900 days, from 1941 to 1944, and hundreds of thousands of its people starved. In 1991 its citizens voted to bring back the old name.
sum: Russia's second city, at the mouth of the Neva on the Baltic Sea, built from 1703 by Peter the Great and the capital of the Russian Empire for two centuries.
